title: First Unique
statement: Implement `solve(items)`. Return the earliest string that appears exactly once. If every string repeats or the list is empty, return the string `none`. A later unique value does not beat an earlier one.
constraints: Scan counts first, then scan the list again
hints: Walk the list a second time and return the first item whose count is 1.
If that walk ends, return none.

approaches.name: Direct
approaches.explanation: The first unique value is not the same as the last time a count flipped to 1, unless you also remember indexes.

editorial: The first unique value is not the same as the last time a count flipped to 1, unless you also remember indexes. Two passes are obvious and linear: counts, then the original order. One pass with a queue of candidates also works if you drop a candidate when it repeats.
